seoTitle: Vertigo Workup in the ED: HINTS Exam, BPPV, Stroke
metaDescription: Dizziness in the ED, fork by fork: timing and triggers, HINTS plus hearing, when MRI beats CT, Dix-Hallpike and Epley, vestibular neuritis, Meniere, TIA.
h1: Dizziness and vertigo: the ED algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM or neurology rotation with a dizzy patient and a resident about to ask what is next: the first moves, timing and triggers, HINTS plus hearing, the gait, MRI versus CT, the BPPV maneuvers, neuritis, Meniere, vestibular migraine and TIA, and the traps.

shortAnswer.lead: Glucose, ECG, drugs and a neurological exam first.
shortAnswer.text: A focal deficit goes straight to the stroke pathway and a thunderclap headache to the headache pathway. No CT first, and no meclizine before the eye exam.

shortAnswer.lead: Sort by timing and triggers, not by the patient's word.
shortAnswer.text: Continuous since onset, triggered attacks, or spontaneous attacks. More than half of patients change their description when asked again minutes later.

shortAnswer.lead: Continuous, with nystagmus: HINTS plus hearing, by a trained examiner.
shortAnswer.text: Peripheral is a corrective saccade on the head impulse, one-way nystagmus and no skew. Any central component, or new one-sided hearing loss, makes it central.

Cannot stand unaided means MRI even with a peripheral HINTS. No nystagmus: grade the gait and test pursuit and saccades; grade 2 or 3, or a central eye sign, means MRI. Walking unaided with normal eye movements: the sources differ on imaging.

Non-contrast CT finds 7 to 28.5% of ischemic strokes in dizzy patients. CT and CTA come first in a reperfusion window, with signs of a bleed or when MRI cannot be done promptly, and a normal early MRI does not exclude a posterior stroke.

shortAnswer.lead: Vestibular neuritis: a few days of suppressant, then rehabilitation.
shortAnswer.text: No longer than 3 to 5 days, a shared decision on steroids within 3 days of onset, no antivirals, and no imaging when the exam confirms a peripheral disorder.

shortAnswer.lead: Triggered attacks: screen for brainstem symptoms, then Dix-Hallpike and Epley.
shortAnswer.text: Posterior canal BPPV gets an Epley toward the positive side at diagnosis, with no imaging and no outpatient suppressants; the horizontal canal gets a barbecue roll or Gufoni maneuver.

shortAnswer.lead: Spontaneous attacks: Meniere, vestibular migraine or TIA.
shortAnswer.text: Ear symptoms point to Meniere, migraine features to vestibular migraine. Vascular risk or a deadly D is a possible posterior TIA: aspirin 300 mg unless contraindicated, MRI, vessel imaging and stroke review within 24 hours.

sections.heading: What do you do first for a dizzy patient in the ED?
sections.intro: Vitals, a fingerstick glucose, a 12-lead ECG, the drug list with a level for phenytoin or carbamazepine, and a neurological exam.

sections.heading: What do the timing, the HINTS, the gait and the MRI tell you?
sections.intro: The forks read the first look, the timing, nystagmus, HINTS plus hearing and gait, the positional tests, the MRI and the audiogram, and the history of spontaneous attacks.

sections.heading: How do you tell peripheral from central vertigo at the bedside?
sections.intro: Timing and triggers first; then nystagmus and HINTS plus hearing, or gait and eye movements when there is no nystagmus; positional tests for triggered attacks; the ear, migraine and vascular history for spontaneous ones.

sections.heading: How are vestibular neuritis, BPPV, Meniere and vestibular migraine treated?
sections.intro: Short-term symptom relief and rehabilitation for neuritis, repositioning maneuvers for BPPV, diet and drugs for Meniere, attack treatment and prevention for vestibular migraine, and a TIA workup for vascular attacks.

sections.heading: When does a dizzy patient need an MRI, and when is CT enough?
sections.intro: MRI with diffusion and vessel imaging whenever the bedside exam cannot call it peripheral; CT first in a reperfusion window, with signs of a bleed, or when MRI cannot be done promptly.

sections.heading: What if the MRI is normal but the exam looks central?
sections.intro: Admit or observe high-risk patients, and repeat the MRI after 3 to 14 days if suspicion persists.

sections.heading: Where does each dizzy patient end up?
sections.intro: Many branches hand on: a focal deficit, a posterior stroke or a cerebellar bleed to the stroke pathway, a cardiac clue to palpitations, chest pain or syncope, a thunderclap headache to the headache pathway.

items.text: Only for continuous dizziness with nystagmus, examined by a clinician trained in HINTS.
Head impulse: a corrective saccade is the peripheral finding; a normal head impulse is central.
Nystagmus: beating one way is peripheral; changing direction with gaze is central.
Test of skew: any skew on the alternate cover test is central.
Hearing: a finger rub for new one-sided loss, a fourth central sign, confirmed by audiometry.
One central component makes the whole result central.
Gait: cannot stand unaided means MRI with DWI, even with a peripheral HINTS.
No trained examiner: a trained specialist or MRI with DWI; CT with or without CTA is insufficient to rule out stroke.

rounds.present: 42-year-old woman with vestibular neuritis: woke yesterday with constant spinning and vomiting, worse with any head movement, after a cold last week. Glucose 101 mg/dL, normal ECG, no focal deficit, no anticonvulsant or aminoglycoside. Constant for 30 hours, so an acute vestibular syndrome. Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating left at rest, stronger on left gaze and still left-beating on right gaze. HINTS peripheral: corrective saccade on the head impulse to the right, normal to the left, no skew; finger rub heard equally; walks unaided, veering right. Plan: no imaging; an antiemetic or meclizine for no longer than 3 to 5 days; a shared decision on short-term steroids, since she is within 3 days of onset; vestibular rehabilitation; referral to a specialist and her primary care physician; return at once for weakness, numbness, double vision, slurred speech or a worse gait.

pimp.q: Why not just ask whether the room spins?
pimp.a: The description is unreliable: more than half change it when asked again minutes later. Timing and triggers sort dizziness.

pimp.q: Corrective saccade on the head impulse. Stroke?
pimp.a: No, that is the peripheral finding. A normal head impulse in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus is the central one.

pimp.q: Why add a hearing check to HINTS?
pimp.a: AICA strokes can cause an abnormal head impulse. Adding new one-sided hearing loss raised sensitivity for AICA strokes from 73.3% to 91.1%.

pimp.q: Why not a CT to rule out a stroke?
pimp.a: It finds only 7 to 28.5% of ischemic strokes in dizzy patients, and a clear CT can falsely reassure. GRACE-3 recommends against routine CT or CTA to tell central from peripheral.

pimp.q: Why not meclizine until the vertigo is gone?
pimp.a: Longer use inhibits central compensation. Suppressants are for no longer than 3 to 5 days, then rehabilitation.

pimp.q: Why no collar or sleeping upright after the Epley?

traps.text: CT first, then the exam. CT finds only 7 to 28.5% of ischemic strokes in dizzy patients.
Meclizine before the eye exam. A vestibular suppressant can take away the nystagmus the exam depends on.
Vomiting means it is not a stroke. With dizziness, nausea and vomiting are the commonest symptoms of a posterior circulation stroke.
Reading the head impulse backwards. The corrective saccade is the peripheral finding.
HINTS without nystagmus. A normal head impulse then falsely suggests a stroke; grade the gait and the eye movements instead.
A normal MRI, so call it neuritis. Early diffusion is falsely negative in about 1 in 5 posterior strokes in the first 24 to 48 hours.
An Epley for horizontal canal BPPV. The horizontal canal needs a barbecue roll or a Gufoni maneuver.
Calling vertigo with new one-sided deafness labyrinthitis before a stroke is excluded. AICA strokes cause exactly this.

faq.a: A three-part bedside exam for continuous vertigo with nystagmus: the head impulse, the direction of nystagmus on gaze, and the test of skew. A corrective saccade, one-way nystagmus and no skew is peripheral; a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or a skew is central. HINTS plus adds new one-sided hearing loss as a fourth central sign, and it needs a trained examiner.

faq.q: How accurate is HINTS for stroke?
faq.a: In the systematic review this pathway cites, HINTS had a sensitivity of 92.7% and a specificity of 91.1%; adding new hearing loss (HINTS plus) gave 95.7% and 80.7%. Done well, it may outperform an early MRI. Untrained emergency physicians do not apply or interpret it reliably, so without a trained examiner a specialist or MRI with DWI stands in.

faq.q: Should a dizzy patient get a CT or an MRI?
faq.a: MRI with diffusion and angiography of the posterior circulation whenever the bedside exam cannot call it peripheral. Non-contrast CT finds only 7 to 28.5% of ischemic strokes in dizzy patients and comes first in a reperfusion window, with signs of a bleed, or when MRI cannot be done promptly; a normal CT excludes nothing. A normal MRI in the first 24 to 48 hours does not exclude a posterior stroke.

faq.q: How do you do the Epley maneuver?
faq.a: Turn the head 45 degrees toward the affected ear and lay the patient back to head-hanging 20 to 30 degrees for 20 to 30 seconds; turn the head 90 degrees to the other side for about 20 seconds; turn a further 90 degrees with the body on its side, nearly face down, for 20 to 30 seconds; then sit up. Repeat the Dix-Hallpike afterward.

With a peripheral HINTS, normal hearing and the patient able to stand unaided: no imaging, an antiemetic or vestibular suppressant for no longer than 3 to 5 days (meclizine 25 to 100 mg a day), a shared decision on short-term steroids within 3 days of onset, no antivirals, vestibular rehabilitation for everyone, and explicit return advice for new neurological symptoms.

faq.q: How do you tell Meniere disease from vestibular migraine?
faq.a: Meniere disease is two or more attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours with a low-frequency hearing loss in one ear tied to the attacks and fluctuating tinnitus or fullness in that ear; audiometry makes it. Vestibular migraine is at least 5 episodes of 5 minutes to 72 hours with a migraine history and migraine features in at least half, and has no diagnostic test.
